source_refs.note: Exercise 4.1, Question 6: RC circuit, charging recalled, discharging deduced; book p. 128, answers p. 303 (PDF 305, printed as item 7)

blocks.prompt: 6 For an RC circuit, recall the differential equation representing the charging of a capacitor. Deduce the differential equation that represents the discharging of the capacitor.
blocks.explanation:
Recall the RC charging model of Example 4(i), then remove the source.
Discharging means the charged capacitor empties through the resistor with no battery in the loop, so \(V_{S} = 0\).
steps:
Given: RC circuit; charging equation from Example 4(i).
To find: the equation for discharging.
Method: recall the charging equation and put \(V_{S} = 0\).

Recall the charging equation
\[R\dfrac{dq}{dt} + \dfrac{q}{C} = V_{S}\]
or
\[RC\dfrac{dq}{dt} = CV_{S} - q\]
Why: Kirchhoff's voltage law \(V_{R} + V_{C} = V_{S}\) with \(V_{R} = R\frac{dq}{dt}\), \(V_{C} = \frac{q}{C}\).

Discharging: no source
\[RC\dfrac{dq}{dt} = -q\]
\[\dfrac{dq}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{RC}q\]
Why: without the battery the loop law becomes \(V_{R} + V_{C} = 0\); the capacitor itself drives the current.

Check:
\(q = q_{0}e^{-t/RC}\) satisfies it (sympy): the charge falls from \(q_{0}\) towards 0, as a discharging capacitor should. The key's answer \(\frac{dq}{dt} = -\frac{1}{RC}q\) (printed as item 7) agrees.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key numbers this answer 7, not 6. Its item 6, \(\frac{dx}{dt} = -\frac{k}{\pi r^{2}}\sqrt{x},\ k > 0\), matches no question of Exercise 4.1, so the answers to Questions 6 and 7 appear as items 7 and 8. The answer itself, \(\frac{dq}{dt} = -\frac{1}{RC}q\), is correct.
